title: Content-Based Instruction — An Introduction to CLIL

pts: Content and Language Integrated Learning teaches subject content — science, geography, current affairs — through the target language.
Both content mastery and language development are genuine, simultaneous aims, not one disguising the other.
This poster introduces the concept; full CLIL methodology is developed in depth in Tier III.

items: Read two descriptions of a lesson on the water cycle (see model language).
For each, note: What content do learners learn? What language do they learn? What do they do?
Decide which is CLIL, and why.
Improve the weaker lesson by adding one language aim and one support.
Teachers bring a science or social science lesson plan and add a language aim.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Lesson A: The teacher reads the textbook paragraph on the water cycle aloud in English. Learners copy the diagram and memorize the definition of ‘evaporation’.

Lesson B: Learners watch water heat in a vessel and describe what they see. They label a diagram, match process words to stages, and explain the cycle to a partner using sequence words (‘First… then… after that…’). A key-word list shows each term in English and Kannada.

blocks.x: Lesson B is CLIL: both content and language are planned and supported. Lesson A uses English, but its only language aim is memorization.

body: Purpose: to show the dual focus. Content: a pair of spectacles; one lens shows a science diagram (content), the other shows a speech bubble with sequence words (language). Through both lenses the learner sees one clear picture. Style: clean, conceptual. Board version: two overlapping circles labelled ‘content’ and ‘language’.

pts: Content: the subject matter itself. Communication: the language needed to engage with it.
Cognition: the thinking skills the content demands. Culture: the awareness the content and language both carry.
Planning against all four Cs, not content alone, distinguishes genuine CLIL from simply lecturing in English.
points.who: Do Coyle, Philip Hood & David Marsh's 4Cs Framework

items: Choose a topic from the science, social science or mathematics textbook.
Fill in a grid with four boxes: content, communication, cognition, culture.
Check that each box is specific: what exactly will learners know, say, think and notice?
Plan one activity that addresses at least three Cs.
Share the grid with a colleague for feedback.
Groups plan the same topic for two different levels and compare.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Content: causes of the monsoon; its importance for farming.
Communication: cause and effect (because, so, as a result); key words (moisture, wind, rainfall).
Cognition: explaining causes; comparing rainfall in two regions from a chart.
Culture: monsoon in farmers’ lives and festivals; how different Indian languages name the seasons.

blocks.x: A lesson planned against content alone becomes a lecture in English. Planning against all four Cs is what makes it CLIL (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010).

body: Purpose: to show the 4Cs Framework. Content: four overlapping circles labelled ‘Content’, ‘Communication’, ‘Cognition’ and ‘Culture’, each with a small icon (a globe, a speech bubble, a lightbulb, a group of people). The overlap at the centre is labelled ‘CLIL lesson’. Style: clear, balanced. Board version: four overlapping circles.

points.h: Language of, for, and through Learning
pts: Language of learning: the subject-specific vocabulary the content requires.
Language for learning: the classroom language needed to engage in tasks — discussing, comparing, hypothesising.
Language through learning: the new language that emerges spontaneously as understanding develops.

items: Read a short content text.
List the language of learning: key subject words and structures.
List the language for learning: what learners must say to do the tasks (compare, discuss, ask).
Predict language through learning: new language that may emerge as learners work.
Plan how to teach the first two, and how to capture the third.
Keep a class ‘language through learning’ list that grows as learners ask for words.
Support: provide the language-for-learning phrases on a card.
Challenge: learners find the key words themselves before the teacher checks.

lines: Language of learning: producer, consumer, predator, prey; X eats Y; Y is eaten by X.
Language for learning: I think… because… Do you agree? What comes next in the chain?
Language through learning (emerging): If the snakes disappear, the frogs will increase.

blocks.x: The third kind cannot be fully planned, but a teacher can notice it, write it on the board and help learners use it again.

body: Purpose: to show the three layers. Content: three panels. The first, ‘of learning’, shows subject words on labels; the second, ‘for learning’, shows learners discussing with speech bubbles; the third, ‘through learning’, shows a new sentence growing like a plant from their discussion. Style: three-panel, warm. Board version: three columns.

items: Padlet (free plan) for a growing ‘through learning’ wall.

blocks.x: A three-column chart on the classroom wall.

pts: Content-based lessons can be cognitively demanding, linguistically demanding, or both — plan support for whichever applies.
Scaffolding techniques from Unit 15 apply directly here, supporting access without lowering the cognitive challenge.
Visual organisers are especially valuable, separating conceptual understanding from purely linguistic demand.

items: Draw a grid: cognitive demand (low to high) on one axis, language demand (low to high) on the other.
Place each task from a planned lesson in the grid.
For high-language tasks, plan language support (word banks, sentence frames, models).
For high-cognitive tasks, plan thinking support (graphic organizers, examples, step-by-step questions).
Check that support does not remove the thinking.
Map a textbook chapter’s end-of-chapter questions on the same grid.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Tasks from a lesson on states of matter:

lines: Label solid, liquid, gas on pictures: low cognitive, low language.
Explain why ice melts: high cognitive, high language. Support: a flow chart and the frame When ice is heated, the particles… so…
Classify ten objects: high cognitive, low language. Support: a sorting table.

blocks.x: A graphic organizer separates understanding from expression: a learner can show that she understands a process on a flow chart before she can explain it in English. Scaffolding techniques from Unit 15 apply directly.

body: Purpose: to show the demand grid. Content: a square divided into four, with axes labelled ‘Thinking’ and ‘Language’. Small task icons sit in different boxes. Arrows show support moving a learner towards the high-thinking, supported-language area. Style: diagrammatic, simple colours. Board version: a four-box grid.

items: Canva (free plan) for graphic organizer templates.

blocks.x: Hand-drawn flow charts, tables and Venn diagrams.

body: Research on bilingual education suggests that concepts learned in one language are available in another: a learner who understands evaporation in Kannada does not have to relearn the concept in English, only the words to express it (Cummins 2000). This is a strong reason to let learners meet new content in their stronger language first.

pts: A single content-based lesson or short unit is a viable, low-risk way to trial this approach before committing further.
Choose content already somewhat familiar to learners in their L1, reducing the compounded cognitive-plus-linguistic load.
This connects to Unit 26's brief introduction of content integration as one of Tier II's core threads.

v: A familiar topic from another subject; visuals

items: Choose a topic learners have already studied in their home language or in another subject.
Set a content aim and a language aim.
Begin with visuals and a quick recall in any language: ‘What do you remember?’
Learners do one English task that uses the content (label, sort, explain to a partner).
End with a short check of both aims.
Run a three-lesson mini-unit once the single lesson has worked.
Support: a bilingual key-word list.
Challenge: learners prepare a short explanation for a younger class.

lines: Content aim: name the planets in order and say one fact about each.
Language aim: comparatives (bigger than, closer to, the hottest).
Task: pairs order planet cards by distance from the Sun, then write three comparisons.
Mercury is closer to the Sun than Earth. Jupiter is the biggest planet.

blocks.x: Familiar content lowers the load: learners are not learning new science and new English at the same time. This connects to Unit 26, which introduced content integration as a thread through Part II.

body: Purpose: to show a low-risk start. Content: a learner dipping one foot into a pool labelled ‘CLIL’, with steps leading down labelled ‘one lesson’, ‘a mini-unit’, ‘a full unit’. Style: light, encouraging. Board version: not applicable.

pts: Assess content understanding and language performance as distinct criteria, so a language gap doesn't mask genuine content mastery.
This previews Unit 46's rubric-design principles, applied specifically to the dual demands of content-based work.
Separate assessment also clarifies feedback — a learner knows which dimension to focus on next.

v: A task with separate content and language criteria

items: Choose a content task, such as explaining a process.
Write two short rubrics: one for content, one for language.
Share both with learners before the task.
Mark the task twice, once with each rubric.
Give feedback that tells learners which area to work on next.
Learners self-assess with one rubric, and the teacher uses the other.
Support: allow a labelled diagram to show content understanding.
Challenge: add a criterion for subject-specific vocabulary.

blocks.x: Task: explain how a seed becomes a plant.

lines: Content: correct stages in order; key process named (germination); cause explained.
Language: sequencing words; present simple; clear sentences.
Deepa: all content correct, several grammar errors. Feedback: excellent science; next, check verb endings.
Rahul: fluent English, one stage missing. Feedback: clear writing; next, reread stage 3.

blocks.x: Without separate criteria, Deepa’s language gaps would hide her understanding. Unit 46 develops rubric design further.

body: Purpose: to show separate assessment. Content: two balance scales side by side, one labelled ‘Content’ and one labelled ‘Language’, each weighing a learner’s work independently. Style: clean. Board version: two columns headed ‘Content’ and ‘Language’.

pts: Simply translating a subject textbook into English rarely produces good CLIL material — genuine adaptation is needed.
This directly extends Unit 13's materials-adaptation principles to subject-content materials specifically.
Graded, simplified content materials exist for many subjects and levels, reducing the adaptation burden.

v: A textbook page from another subject

items: Take a page from a science or social science textbook.
Mark words and structures that may block understanding.
Adapt the text: shorter sentences, key words in bold, a diagram, a glossary.
Add tasks before, during and after reading.
Check that the content has not been lost in simplification.
Compare the adapted text with a graded content reader on the same topic.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Original (written for this book): Photosynthesis is the process whereby green plants utilize solar energy to synthesize carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen as a by-product. Adapted:

lines: Green plants make their own food. This is called photosynthesis. Plants need sunlight, water and carbon dioxide. They make sugar. They give out oxygen.
Added: a labelled diagram of a leaf; a glossary with Kannada or Hindi equivalents; a task to complete a flow chart.

blocks.x: The principles of materials adaptation in Unit 13 apply here, with one extra check: the content must remain accurate.

body: Purpose: to show adaptation. Content: a dense block of textbook text passing through hands that reshape it into short sentences, a diagram and a glossary box. Style: practical, clear. Board version: not applicable.

items: DIKSHA (free, Government of India) for state and NCERT textbook content in several languages.
Oxford Read and Discover or similar graded content readers (paid) where available.

blocks.x: A photocopy of the textbook page annotated by hand.

pts: Effective CLIL often benefits from collaboration between language teachers and subject specialists, where both roles exist separately.
Where one teacher covers both roles, deliberately separating language-focus and content-focus planning time helps.
This collaboration model is developed further in Tier III's full CLIL methodology.

items: Pair a language teacher with a subject teacher.
The subject teacher identifies the key concepts for a topic.
The language teacher identifies the language learners will need.
Together, plan one lesson that serves both.
Where one teacher covers both roles, plan in two separate sittings: first content, then language.
The English teacher uses a science topic in an English lesson in the same week that the science teacher teaches it.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Science teacher: Key concepts: conductors and insulators. Common confusion: all metals are conductors, but not all conductors are metals.
English teacher: Language: classifying (X is a… because…); negatives (does not allow…); adjectives ending in -ive (conductive).
Joint lesson: learners test objects with a simple circuit and classify them, reporting in full sentences.

body: Ask a science or social science colleague which topic learners find hardest to understand this term. Plan one English lesson on that topic, using familiar content, a graphic organizer and a key-word list. Afterwards, ask your colleague whether learners understood the topic better.

dek: Unit 37 of 100: teaching real subject content through English integrates language learning with genuine cognitive demand — a first look at a methodology explored fully in Tier III.

aims.x: This unit introduces content-based instruction, and in particular Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL), in which learners study real subject matter through English. It is a first look. Unit 55 returns to CLIL in full and shows how to plan a complete content unit. Here the aim is to understand the core ideas and to try one light-touch lesson.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain what CLIL is and how it differs from teaching a subject in English without planning for language;
plan a lesson using the 4Cs Framework of content, communication, cognition and culture;
distinguish the language of, for and through learning;
analyse the cognitive and linguistic demands of a content task and plan support for each;
design a short, low-risk content-based lesson;
assess content and language with separate criteria;
adapt subject materials rather than simply translating them;
plan collaboration between language and subject teachers.

why: Why this matters. Language taught only as a subject in its own right can feel disconnected from anything real. Content integration gives language a genuine reason to be used.

background.x: Content-based instruction has roots in several traditions. Bernard Mohan (1986) argued that language and content should be integrated because we learn language through using it to learn about the world. Brinton, Snow and Wesche (1989) described content-based models in North American schools and universities. In Europe, the term CLIL was adopted in the 1990s for approaches in which a subject such as geography or science is taught through an additional language, with planned attention to both. The central framework for CLIL planning is the 4Cs of Do Coyle, Philip Hood and David Marsh (2010): content, communication, cognition and culture.

Two ideas from Jim Cummins help to explain why CLIL needs careful planning. The first is the distinction between everyday conversational fluency and the academic language needed for school learning, which takes much longer to develop (Cummins 1979, 2000). A learner who chats easily in English may still struggle to explain photosynthesis in English. The second is Cummins’s model of tasks as more or less cognitively demanding and more or less supported by context. CLIL teachers try to keep the thinking demanding while adding context: pictures, diagrams, demonstrations and the learners’ own knowledge. Research on CLIL classrooms (for example, Dalton-Puffer 2007) shows that much depends on how teachers structure talk; simply using English as the medium is not enough.

India has a long history of teaching subjects through English, often without the planned language support that defines CLIL. Many learners in English-medium schools memorize science answers they do not fully understand. The NEP 2020 recommends that the home language or mother tongue be the medium of instruction wherever possible until at least Grade 5, and encourages bilingual teaching and materials (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). The NCF 2023 also stresses multilingual learning (NCERT 2023). CLIL, well understood, fits this vision. Learners can meet a concept first in their stronger language, then work with it in English; key terms can be shown in Kannada, Hindi or Tamil alongside English. In the English lesson, a light-touch CLIL approach gives language a real reason to be used: learners are finding out about something, not only practising forms.

items: Content check. A short diagram, sort or explanation that shows understanding without heavy language demands.
Language check. A task that uses the target language of and for learning, assessed with its own criteria.
Learner reflection. Learners note one thing they learned about the subject and one thing they learned about English.
Teacher collaboration. Review a jointly planned lesson with the subject teacher: did both aims succeed?
In your school, is English used to teach other subjects? How is language supported?
What topics from other subjects do your learners already know well?
Which Cs do you usually plan for? Which do you neglect?
How could learners’ home languages help them understand new content?
Do your assessments ever confuse a language gap with a gap in understanding?
Which subject teacher could you work with this term?

terms.def: A planning framework for CLIL that asks teachers to integrate content, communication, cognition and culture in each unit (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010); for example, a science lesson on the water cycle also plans its language and thinking demands.

The vocabulary, grammar and text structures used in school subjects and study, such as defining, comparing and explaining, as distinct from everyday conversational language; many learners need explicit support to master it.
The level of thinking a task requires, from recalling and describing to analysing and evaluating; CLIL lessons plan the language needed for each level.
An approach in which a subject such as science or geography is taught through an additional language, with planned attention to both content and language.
Language teaching organized around subject matter or themes rather than a language syllabus, so that learners acquire language while learning content.
A visual framework, such as a table, flowchart, Venn diagram or mind map, that helps learners organize ideas or information from a text before speaking or writing.
In the CLIL Language Triptych, the language learners need to take part in learning, such as asking questions, working in groups and presenting (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010).
In the CLIL Language Triptych, the subject-specific language needed to understand and express content, such as the terms for photosynthesis (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010).
In the CLIL Language Triptych, the new language that emerges as learners think, discuss and learn content (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010).

Changing published or existing materials to suit a particular class, by omitting, adding, simplifying, reordering or personalizing content; for example, replacing a foreign setting in a textbook dialogue with a local one.
